name: Fire when everything is soaked
summary: Rain does not reach the inside of a standing dead branch. Getting at that dry core — by height, by splitting, by feathering — is the whole technique.

substitutes: dead branch still on the tree

steps.text: NEVER take wood off the ground. Ground wood is a sponge and it is rotten. Take dead branches still attached to a standing tree — snap-test them: they should CRACK, not bend.
Go UP. The higher a dead branch is, the drier it is, and the small dead twigs low on a conifer trunk under the living canopy are often bone dry in steady rain.
BATON to the heart. Split a wrist-thick piece by driving your knife through it with a club. The outer centimetre is wet; the heartwood inside is dry, and that dry core is your kindling.
steps.why: This is the whole insight. In a rain-soaked forest the dry wood is not somewhere else — it is INSIDE the wet wood, a few millimetres in.

steps.text: FEATHER STICKS. Take a split dry stave and shave long thin curls down its length, leaving them attached in a shaggy head. Three or four good ones will take a flame where loose shavings blow away.
Shave the curls THIN and keep the blade at a shallow angle, riding the grain. A thick curl is kindling; a paper-thin one is tinder.

Look for FATWOOD — resin-saturated heartwood at the stump or knots of dead conifers. It is heavy, smells strongly of turpentine and lights wet. Birch bark does the same and peels off a living tree in sheets.
Build ON a dry platform of split wood or bark, never on wet ground, and build a lean-to or hold your body over it to keep rain off while it establishes.
Once it burns, stack wet wood AROUND the fire to dry for the next hour's fuel.

verify: A snapped branch cracks sharply and shows pale dry wood at the break. A dull thud and a damp dark break means put it back.
Feather curls that stay springy and translucent when you bend them are dry; ones that flop and stay bent are not.
The fire keeps burning without you shielding it — before that, it is not established, whatever it looks like.
limits: It buys you dry FUEL. It cannot compensate for a bad tinder bundle, a wet lay, or an ignition source you cannot work with cold hands.
In sustained rain with no shelter over the fire, an established fire can still be drowned. Roof it before you need to.
It needs an edge. Without a knife or axe, batoning and feathering are both off the table and you are down to whatever is already dry.
cautions: Batoning with a folding knife can break it. Use a fixed blade if you have one, strike the SPINE over the widest part, and never near the lock.
Cold, wet hands lose fine motor control fast — do the knife work early, while you can still feel your fingers.
Do not strip bark all the way around a living birch; it girdles and kills the tree. Take from fallen trunks or in patches.
